title: Unexpected asymmetric Qinghai–Tibetan wildlife dietary response to anthropause: Rapid initial shifts and a slow return
content:
This study provides rare multigenerational evidence that wildlife established in human-modified habitats responds asymmetrically to changing human activity. Dietary shifts were rapid when disturbance declined, whereas dietary divergence re-emerged more slowly after disturbance resumed, suggesting that temporary reductions in human disturbance may have lasting ecological effects.


Abstract

Understanding how wildlife adapts to changes in human activity intensity is crucial for effective conservation in human-modified ecosystems. The 3-year COVID-19 related anthropause in China created an unprecedented experimental setting to examine details of the ecological impact of human absence from otherwise disturbed habitats. We investigated the ecological impact of the anthropause on roadside small mammals by testing if and how their diets changed over a 7-year period spanning before (2018–2019), during (2020–2022) and after (2023–2024) the anthropause, and whether these changes reflected temporary or lasting shifts in human activity. We assessed human impact on a keystone Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau wildlife taxon, pikas (Ochotona spp.), by recording and comparing their diets (using faecal DNA metabarcoding) from roadside and road-distant (non-disturbed) populations. We coupled the dietary differences results with vegetation structure and traffic density records to assess the effects of human activity intensity and infrastructure on dietary composition. Before the anthropause, roadside populations consumed dicot-rich diets distinct from nearby undisturbed meadow populations. During the reduced human activity of the anthropause, roadside pika diets rapidly converged with those of undisturbed populations within a single year, decoupling from local roadside vegetation compositions. After human activity resumed, dietary divergence between roadside and natural populations reappeared slowly across generations. These data reveal an asymmetric, multigenerational response: rapid convergence under reduced disturbance, followed by a slow divergence with the resumption of disturbance. Regression analyses show that traffic density was associated with dietary divergence between habitats and with diet–vegetation dissimilarity in roadside populations. These multigenerational data demonstrate that wildlife in human-modified landscapes remain sensitive to changes in human activity, even after prolonged exposure. Importantly, these asymmetric responses suggest that temporary reductions in human disturbance, such as traffic management, can yield lasting biodiversity benefits in increasingly human-dominated landscapes, and these responses should be explored as part of broader conservation efforts in human-modified ecosystems.

中文摘要

人类活动强度的动态变化深刻影响着野生动物的行为与资源利用，但长期生活在人类干扰环境中的动物如何响应干扰强度的起伏，目前仍缺乏长期、连续的实证证据。新冠疫情防控期间人类活动的大幅减少（即“人类活动暂停”，Anthropause），为检验野生动物对干扰强度变化的响应机制提供了一个难得的准实验条件。 本研究以青藏高原代表性小型哺乳动物鼠兔（Ochotona spp.）为研究对象，整合 2018—2024 年连续 7 年的监测数据，系统对比了新冠疫情防控（跨城人员流动受限期）之前（2018—2019 年）、期间（2020—2022 年）和之后（2023—2024 年）公路沿线种群与远离道路草甸种群的食性差异。研究基于粪便 DNA 宏条形码技术测定鼠兔食性，并结合同期植被组成和交通流量数据，深入解析食性动态与人类活动强度之间的定量关系。 研究发现，疫情前路边鼠兔种群食性以双子叶植物为主，与邻近草甸种群存在显著分化。疫情期间，随着人类活动大幅减少，路边种群的食性在短短一个世代内迅速向草甸种群趋同，同时与其所在路边的植被组成拉大了差异；而在疫情后人类活动恢复常态时，路边种群食性并未随之迅速复原，而是经历了数个世代才缓慢恢复至疫情前的分化状态。 这种响应呈现出显著的不对称性：对干扰减弱的响应极为迅速，而对干扰恢复的响应则明显滞后。机制分析进一步表明，交通流量越大，路边与草甸种群间的食性分化越显著，且路边种群的食性越趋近于当地路边植被组成。 这项长达 7 年的连续监测表明，即使长期生活在人类改造环境中的野生动物，其资源利用策略仍具备高度的可塑性，且对干扰“消退”与“重现”的响应具有非对称特征。这一发现意味着，阶段性或周期性地降低交通等人类干扰，能够产生比干扰暂停期本身更持久的生态效应，为人类主导景观下的野生动物保护与管理提供了新的科学思路。
